title: Two spirits talk
hookLine: two mountain spirits check the Buddha's character before they go to meet him
last: AS A MOTHER HER ONLY CHILD.

lines: A HOLY NIGHT ON THE MOUNTAIN.
cards: Before you hire someone, you call their references. Before you try a new doctor, you ask a friend: is she any good? Not her diploma.
Her. Does she listen? Is she honest?
The ninth poem of the Sutta Nipata is a reference check, done by two yakkhas, nature spirits of the hills. It's the fifteenth night of the month, a holy day.
One spirit, Satagira, says to his friend: tonight's a special night. Let's go see the teacher Gotama. And his friend Hemavata, from the Himalaya, says: wait.

teach.h: WAIT: TELL ME ABOUT HIM FIRST
teach.b: Hemavata's questions come in a steady rhythm, and Satagira answers every one. Is his mind well disposed toward all beings? It is.
Does he master his reactions to what he likes and what he doesn't? He does. Does he take what isn't given?
He doesn't. Is he restrained toward living things, never careless, never neglecting meditation? He is.
Does he lie? Speak harshly? Carry tales between people?
Chatter about nothing? No, no, no and no. His words, Satagira says, are measured and full of sense.
Is he free from craving, his mind clear, with the eye that sees the truth? Yes. Notice what Hemavata doesn't ask.
Not: can he do miracles? Not: how well-known is he? Not even: what does he teach?

teach.h: HOW HE TREATS BEINGS, HOW HE SPEAKS
teach.b: Every question is about character: how he treats beings, how he speaks, whether his mind is steady.
That's the test the poem sets for a teacher. And notice Satagira. He doesn't exaggerate or sell.
He answers honestly, one question at a time, and in doing it he speaks well of someone good.
Then the two spirits go down the mountain and ask the Buddha their own questions. What does the world arise in? In six, he says: the six senses.

At the end, the spirits decide to travel from village to village and mountain to mountain, honoring the Buddha and the teaching. A good reputation, carried by a friend's honest words, became a journey.

how: Buddhist texts encourage people to examine a teacher's conduct and speech over time before placing trust in them, and on uposatha days, the holy days of the lunar month, lay Buddhists may visit a temple, keep extra precepts and hear teaching.

o: a wandering monk who lives in caves
a hungry ghost of someone who has died
a nature spirit, like those of the hills

games.q: the two spirits: tap the pairs.
p: says: let's go see the teacher

s: Hemavata asks whether the Buddha can perform miracles
every question is about character: kindness, honesty, speech, a steady mind.
Satagira answers each question honestly, one at a time
he speaks well of the Buddha without exaggerating.
the yakkhas end by traveling to honor the Buddha
from village to village and mountain to mountain.

games.q: you're Hemavata. your friend wants you to meet a well-known teacher tonight. what do you ask first?
o: how many followers does he have?
is his mind well disposed toward all beings?
games.why: Hemavata's questions are all about character: kindness to beings, honest speech, a steady mind.

practice: Choose someone you respect, a teacher, a coworker, a relative, and quietly ask Hemavata's questions about them: are they kind to people, do they tell the truth, do they stay out of gossip?
Let honest answers come, not flattery, and notice which ones make you glad.

wordCard.voice: yakkha. Hemavata asks about the Buddha's character, Satagira answers honestly, and a good word, well spoken, sends them down the mountain. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali yakkha (Sanskrit yaksha): a nature spirit of trees, hills or wild places, sometimes kind, sometimes fierce.

carryVoice: Your line: they spoke well of him. An honest good word can start a journey. Until tomorrow.
